what_it_does: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) is a technique for rendering realistic 3D scenes by representing the scene as millions of fuzzy blobs (Gaussians) and projecting them onto a 2D screen — but doing this on a GPU is slow because the steps (sorting the blobs by depth, then coloring pixels) must happen one after another and produce large temporary data structures. GSAcc is a custom hardware accelerator that breaks this sequential bottleneck by speculatively guessing each blob's depth before the sort is fully done, so preprocessing and sorting can overlap in time. It also redesigns the rendering pipeline around each individual Gaussian blob rather than each pixel, so all stages can run at the same time without needing to store large intermediate buffers. Dedicated hardware units handle sorting and pixel coloring more efficiently than a general-purpose GPU. The result, based on the abstract, is claimed to be faster rendering with lower memory use, though exact numbers are not available here.
